checks.prompt: A team has a working retrieval pipeline — fetch documents, render a prompt, call the model, parse the answer — and is now adding a feature: the assistant should be able to call tools repeatedly, an unknown number of times, until it decides it has enough, and a human must approve any tool call that writes data. They ask whether to rebuild the retrieval pipeline in this library too. What is the right advice and why?
checks.explanation: The dividing line is control flow. A straight line — retrieve, prompt, call, parse — is what forward-only pipe composition is for, and rebuilding it as a graph adds wiring for nothing. What pipes cannot express is a backward edge: a loop that runs an unknown number of times, with state accumulating across iterations and a point where execution can pause for a human and later resume. That is this library's whole reason to exist, and it is why the older black-box agent executor it replaces is legacy: the loop was hidden and could not be inspected, customised or resumed.
options: Keep the retrieval pipeline as a linear composition and build the new feature here. The deciding property is that the new feature is a loop of unknown length with a state that accumulates and a pause for approval, none of which a forward-only pipeline can express; the retrieval pipeline is a straight line and gains nothing but wiring from being rebuilt as a graph
Rebuild both here. Mixing two orchestration models in one codebase is the real cost, and a straight-line flow is simply a graph with no branches, so there is no downside

Build neither here: the loop can be expressed by piping the model stage into itself and adding a conditional wrapper, and approval is a concern for the user interface rather than the orchestration layer
Keep both as linear compositions and use the older agent-executor abstraction for the loop, since that is the supported way to run tools repeatedly

checks.prompt: Describe this library as a runnable flowchart: name the four moving parts, say exactly what a node receives and what it returns, explain what decides where execution goes next, and explain how the classic tool-using agent loop is drawn in these terms — including which single element makes it a loop rather than a pipeline. Then explain what compiling the graph gives you.
checks.expected: A correct answer must name and connect four things. (1) A single shared state object, described by a schema, that flows through the whole graph. (2) Nodes, which are plain functions taking the current state and returning a PARTIAL update — only the keys they changed — rather than a whole new state; the library merges that delta back in. (3) The per-field merge rules that govern that merge: replacing the field is the default, and accumulating (appending to a list of messages or results) is opt-in per field. (4) Edges, which decide the next step: a plain edge always goes to the same place, and a conditional edge is a function that reads the state and returns where to go, which is how branching happens. Entry and exit are marked by sentinels. The agent loop must be drawn concretely: a node that calls the model, a conditional edge asking whether the model requested a tool, a node that executes tools, and — the load-bearing element — an edge from the tools node BACK to the model node. That backward edge is what makes it a cycle and is exactly what a forward-only pipeline cannot express; the conditional edge's other branch reaches the exit sentinel and is what lets the loop terminate. Compiling must be described as freezing the graph into a runnable that can be invoked, streamed and, when given a persistence backend, snapshotted after each step so a run can be paused, resumed or continued later. Noting that the state is treated as immutable — emit a delta, do not mutate the input — is a plus.

checks.prompt: An agent's conversation history keeps disappearing: after the tools node runs, the earlier messages are gone and the model re-asks for information it already has. The team's state schema declares a messages field and every node returns `{"messages": [new_message]}`. The team's proposed fix is to have each node return the entire message list it was given plus the new entry. Diagnose the bug and evaluate the fix.
checks.explanation: This is the single most common bug in the library. A state field is overwritten by each update unless you declare a merge rule for it, so a list-valued field without one keeps only the newest node's contribution. The fix belongs in the schema — declare that the field accumulates — not in the nodes. Making each node rebuild the whole list works by accident, scatters the accumulation logic, and stops working as soon as more than one node or branch contributes, which is exactly what the per-field merge rule exists to handle.
options: The field has no accumulating merge rule, so the default — replace — throws the old list away on every update. The correct fix is to annotate the field with an appending merge rule; the team's proposal papers over it by making every node reconstruct the whole list, which fights the merge machinery, duplicates the accumulation logic in each node and breaks the moment two branches update the field
The bug is that nodes must return the whole state, and the team's fix is therefore correct: partial updates are only supported for scalar fields, not for lists
The bug is that the tools node runs before the model node has committed its update, so the fix is to add an explicit edge forcing the order; merge rules affect only persistence, not in-memory state
The bug is that the messages field is being read by reference and mutated in place, so the fix is to deep-copy the state at the start of every node; merge rules would not help

checks.prompt: Implement the graph runtime. Define `START = "__start__"` and `END = "__end__"`, an exception class `GraphRecursionError(RuntimeError)`, and a `StateGraph(reducers=None)` whose `reducers` maps a state key to a two-argument merge function. Give it `add_node(name, fn)`, `add_edge(a, b)`, `add_conditional_edges(src, router)`, `set_entry_point(name)` and `merge(state, update)`, plus `compile(checkpointer=None)` returning an object with `invoke(state, config=None, recursion_limit=25)`. `merge` returns a NEW dict: for each key in the update, apply that key's merge function to the existing value and the new one when the key has a merge function AND is already present in the state, and otherwise overwrite. `invoke` starts at the entry point and repeats: call the current node's function with the current state, merge the partial update it returns, then move to the destination given by that node's router if it has one and by its static edge otherwise, stopping when the destination is `END`. It must never mutate the dict it was given. Raise `GraphRecursionError` if `recursion_limit` node executions pass without reaching `END`, and `ValueError` if a destination is neither `END` nor a defined node. When a `checkpointer` (any dict-like keyed by thread id) was passed to `compile`, `invoke` requires a thread id at `config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` and raises `ValueError` without one; it starts from the saved state for that thread with the passed-in state merged into it by the same rules, and saves the final state back under that thread. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Each block asserts one thing the library actually promises. The first pair is the merge rule: two nodes written identically behave completely differently depending on whether their field has an accumulating rule — with one the log grows, without one it is clobbered — and that is the bug behind every report of vanishing conversation history. The cycle shows why a graph beats a pipeline: the tools node's edge points backwards, the conditional edge is the only way out, and the loop runs exactly as many times as the state requires. The step cap is the backstop for the cycle you get wrong, and refusing an unknown destination turns a router typo into an error at the point of the mistake instead of a silent dead end. Finally, persistence is keyed by a thread id, which is why the same id continues a conversation and a new one starts clean — and why forgetting it is an error rather than a quietly fresh state.
checks.test:
import operator

# A field with a merge rule accumulates; a field without one is REPLACED by each
# node's update. Both nodes are written the same way -- the difference is the rule.
graph = StateGraph(reducers={"log": operator.add})
graph.add_node("greet", lambda s: {"log": [f"hello {s['name']}"], "count": 1})
graph.add_node("shout", lambda s: {"log": ["GOODBYE"], "count": s["count"] + 1})
graph.set_entry_point("greet")
graph.add_edge("greet", "shout")
graph.add_edge("shout", END)
app = graph.compile()
start = {"name": "ada", "log": [], "count": 0}
final = app.invoke(start)
assert final["log"] == ["hello ada", "GOODBYE"], final
assert final["count"] == 2, final
assert final["name"] == "ada", "a key no node touched survives"
assert start == {"name": "ada", "log": [], "count": 0}, "the caller's dict is not mutated"

# The same graph with the rule removed: the accumulating field is clobbered, which
# is exactly the bug that makes conversation history disappear.
plain = StateGraph()
plain.add_node("greet", lambda s: {"log": ["hello"]})
plain.add_node("shout", lambda s: {"log": ["GOODBYE"]})
plain.set_entry_point("greet")
plain.add_edge("greet", "shout")
plain.add_edge("shout", END)
assert plain.compile().invoke({"log": []})["log"] == ["GOODBYE"]

# The cycle: think, act, come back, and stop only when the router says so.
FACTS = {"capital": "Paris", "population": "67M", "currency": "EUR"}


def agent_node(state):
    missing = [k for k in FACTS if k not in state["facts"]]
    if missing:
        return {"next_tool": missing[0], "scratch": [f"want {missing[0]}"]}
    return {"next_tool": None, "scratch": ["answering"]}


def tools_node(state):
    key = state["next_tool"]
    return {"facts": {key: FACTS[key]}, "scratch": [f"looked up {key}"]}


loop = StateGraph(reducers={"facts": lambda a, b: {**a, **b}, "scratch": operator.add})
loop.add_node("agent", agent_node)
loop.add_node("tools", tools_node)
loop.set_entry_point("agent")
loop.add_conditional_edges("agent", lambda s: "tools" if s["next_tool"] else END)
loop.add_edge("tools", "agent")
done = loop.compile().invoke({"facts": {}, "next_tool": None, "scratch": []})
assert done["facts"] == FACTS, done
assert done["scratch"].count("answering") == 1, done
assert len([s for s in done["scratch"] if s.startswith("looked up")]) == 3, done

# A backward edge with no way out is caught by the step cap rather than hanging.
spin = StateGraph(reducers={"n": operator.add})
spin.add_node("a", lambda s: {"n": 1})
spin.set_entry_point("a")
spin.add_edge("a", "a")
try:
    spin.compile().invoke({"n": 0}, recursion_limit=10)
except GraphRecursionError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unterminated cycle must be stopped")

# A router that returns a destination nobody defined is a wiring bug, reported here
# rather than silently going nowhere.
typo = StateGraph()
typo.add_node("a", lambda s: {})
typo.set_entry_point("a")
typo.add_conditional_edges("a", lambda s: "toolz")
try:
    typo.compile().invoke({})
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown destination must be refused")

# Persistence: the same conversation id continues where it left off, a new one
# starts clean, and no id at all with persistence configured is an error.
saver = {}
chat = StateGraph(reducers={"messages": operator.add})
chat.add_node("reply", lambda s: {"messages": [f"bot saw {len(s['messages'])}"]})
chat.set_entry_point("reply")
chat.add_edge("reply", END)
durable = chat.compile(checkpointer=saver)

one = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}}
durable.invoke({"messages": ["hi"]}, one)
second = durable.invoke({"messages": ["again"]}, one)
assert second["messages"] == ["hi", "bot saw 1", "again", "bot saw 3"], second
fresh = durable.invoke({"messages": ["hi"]}, {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t2"}})
assert fresh["messages"] == ["hi", "bot saw 1"], fresh
assert saver["t1"]["messages"] == second["messages"]
try:
    durable.invoke({"messages": ["hi"]})
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("persistence needs a thread id")

# Without a checkpointer, every call starts from what it was given.
assert app.invoke(start)["log"] == ["hello ada", "GOODBYE"]

checks.prompt: A team ships an agent built with the one-line prebuilt helper and an in-memory persistence backend. Three problems arrive: after a deployment, every user's conversation has reset; they now need a validation step between the model and the tools, plus a retry path, and cannot see where to put it; and the progress display shows nothing useful because they subscribed to a stream and printed whatever arrived. What is the correct assessment?
checks.explanation: Three independent lessons. The in-memory persistence backend is for notebooks and tests — it vanishes with the process, and durable state needs a file- or database-backed one. The prebuilt agent builder is convenient precisely because it hides the graph, which is also its limit: the moment you need a validation node, a reflection step or non-standard routing, you build the graph yourself. And streaming is not one thing: you choose between the full state after each step, the delta from each node, or the model's tokens, and picking the wrong one is the usual reason streaming 'doesn't show what I expected'.
options: The in-memory backend is a development convenience and loses everything when the process exits — durable persistence needs an on-disk or database-backed one. The prebuilt helper hides the graph, which is fine until you need custom routing or extra nodes; at that point you drop down and build the graph by hand, which is the whole point of the library. And streaming has distinct modes — the full state each step, only each node's delta, or the model's tokens — so the display depends on choosing the one matching what you want to show

All three are configuration: the in-memory backend persists if a thread id is supplied, the prebuilt helper accepts extra nodes through its arguments, and the stream emits every mode at once so the display problem is a filtering bug in their own code

The conversations reset because the thread id was regenerated on deployment rather than because of the backend; the prebuilt helper cannot be extended at all, so custom routing means changing library; and streaming only ever yields the final answer

Persistence is unrelated to the backend choice and is governed by the step cap; the prebuilt helper should be subclassed to add nodes; and the stream shows nothing useful because intermediate steps are only observable through an external tracing product

checks.prompt: Three teams ask what to use. Team A: a nightly job that summarises documents — fetch, prompt, call, parse. Team B: a research assistant that plans, calls tools in a loop, reflects on its own output, sometimes revisits an earlier step, must survive a restart mid-run and pause for human approval. Team C: a small team that wants a multi-agent system with named roles and delegated tasks working out of the box, and does not want to design a control flow. Recommend for each and justify from the requirements. Then explain the sense in which the answer for Team B and the answer for Team A are complements rather than competitors.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all three against their stated requirements. Team A: a linear composition in the pipe-based framework — the flow is a straight line with no state to accumulate, no branching and no loop, so the graph runtime is wiring for nothing; for a single model call the raw provider SDK would do. Team B: this library — every one of their requirements is one of its features, and the answer should map them: a loop of unknown length is a cycle, revisiting an earlier step is a backward edge, surviving a restart mid-run is snapshotting state after each step keyed by a conversation id, and pausing for approval is the interrupt mechanism that surfaces state to a human and resumes afterwards. Streaming intermediate progress is a bonus for a long-running research task. Team C: a higher-level, opinionated role-and-task or conversational multi-agent framework, because they explicitly do not want to design the control flow; the trade must be stated — less control over the exact loop and state in exchange for far less wiring — and the answer should note that this library is deliberately lower-level and gives you primitives, not roles, so choosing it would mean building the choreography yourself. The complement argument must be made concretely: the pipe framework supplies the components — models, prompts, retrievers, parsers — while the graph runtime supplies the control flow between them, and a node in the graph is very often one of those linear compositions; they operate at different levels rather than competing, which is why a common production stack uses one for components, the other for control flow, and a tracing product alongside both.
